newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Intermagnetics sees FRIGC FR-12 gaining. [CORRECTED 19:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Intermagnetics sees FRIGC FR-12 gaining. [CORRECTED 19:40 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline to make clear company sees FRIGC FR-12 gaining, not Freon R-12)
By Gilles Castonguay

Intermagnetics General Corp plans to capture up to half the market for air conditioner refrigerants in used vehicles in the next five years by promoting a cheaper and safer substitute for the environmentally dangerous Freon R-12, according to its president, Carl Rosner.
"We are convined that it has major market potential," he told Reuters on Monday.

Rosner said Intermagnetics had launched a national advertising campaign to convince people who own cars and trucks built before 1994 to switch to FRIGC FR-12 when they replenish the Freon in their air conditioners.
If the campaign is successful, sales from a market worth "hundreds of millions of dollars" could contribute up to 10 percent of the company's revenues in fiscal 1998, he said.
"It could become the fastest growing segment of our business." Rosner added.
Scott Davidson, an analyst at First Albany Corp, considered the estimate conservative.
"I see it between 15 and 20 percent," he said.
In March, Intermagnetics reported flat share earnings on revenues of $18.2 million for the third quarter ended February 23 against a profit of $0.06 on $21.2 million a year ago.
Rosner said he did not know if sales in the new product would have any impact on the next quarter's earnings.
FRIGC is the first product that Intermagnetics, known for its superconductive magnets used in magnetic resonance imaging at hospitals, is selling to the consumer market.
Its wholly-owned subsidiary, InterCool Energy Corp, is focusing on used car owners because automobile manufacturers are already using a refrigerant called R-134A for new models.
AlliedSignal Inc is providing one of the components used to make FRIGC, while Pennzoil Co is helping distribute it. Other distributors are being sought.
Rosner said "tens of millions" of vehicles will likely need to replenish up to three pounds of Freon this year.
He said InterCool would take advantage of the dwindling supply of Freon, whose production and import is banned in the United States due to the damage it causes to the ozone layer.
He said FRIGC cost up to $14 a pound, while Freon cost up to $30.
Rosner estimated the shortfall in Freon would total up to eight million pounds this year, "and its going to grow every year".
He said he expected the subsidiary to capture in the next three to five years up to 50 percent of the market of vehicle owners replenishing their refrigerant.

But Davidson at First Albany said Rosner might be too optimistic in his forecast on the dwindling supply of Freon. "There are some people who tend to believe that there is enough Freon that is stockpiled," he said.
Davidson said FRIGC had nevertheless been well received by trucking companies that began using the refrigerant last year when it was partially introduced.
"There has been positive feedback," he said. "Now they (Intermagnetics) have to get the public to know about it.
"They definitely have a leg up since there is no other product like it out there," he added.
On Monday, the company's stock was trading up 5/16 at 12-5/16 on the American Stock Exchange.
First Call's consensus among analysts forecast a profit of $0.13 a share for the fourth quarter.
